final_story.title: LLM-based Autonomous Agent Collaboration Framework: Enabling Accessible Task Coordination via Adapted Pretraining and Pruning
final_story.abstract: Autonomous agent collaboration using large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex tasks, but current frameworks are often resource-intensive, lack theoretical grounding, and are inaccessible to many practitioners. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework for LLM-based autonomous agent collaboration that prioritizes efficiency and accessibility. Our solution adapts the pretraining pipeline of agent models to embed collaborative task signals, uses the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) to model inter-agent decision dynamics for better alignment, and applies Globally Unique Movement (GUM) pruning to optimize agent efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that our framework enables effective collaboration on multi-agent tasks under constrained computational resources (single GPU), reducing costs while maintaining performance. This work democratizes access to LLM-based agent collaboration systems, making them feasible for researchers and practitioners with limited compute.
final_story.problem_framing: We reframe the narrative of LLM-based autonomous agent collaboration from maximizing individual agent capability to optimizing collaborative efficiency and accessibility. Current collaborative agent systems require extensive computational resources—from large model sizes to high-bandwidth interaction—making them inaccessible to most researchers. Additionally, the lack of theoretical models for agent interaction dynamics hinders the design of effective collaborative tasks. By leveraging insights from scaling laws and efficiency techniques, we aim to show that meaningful agent collaboration can be achieved even with limited resources, opening doors to broader adoption of collaborative agent frameworks.
final_story.gap_pattern: Existing LLM-based agent collaboration frameworks fail to address three critical gaps: First, they rely on unoptimized, large agent models that demand high compute, limiting accessibility. Second, there is no theoretical understanding of how agents’ decisions evolve during collaboration, leading to suboptimal task alignment. Third, collaborative task signals are not integrated into the pretraining process, forcing agents to learn collaboration post-hoc with extra cost. These gaps prevent the democratization of agent collaboration systems, leaving them confined to well-resourced teams.
final_story.solution: Our framework addresses these gaps by integrating three key technical adaptations tailored to agent collaboration. First, we modify the transformer-based agent pretraining pipeline to include collaborative task signals (shared goal embedding, turn-taking dynamics) so agents learn to collaborate from the start, reducing post-hoc fine-tuning costs. Second, we use the NTK framework to model the gradient descent dynamics of agent interaction—this helps predict how agents adjust decisions to align with team goals, providing a theoretical foundation for collaborative task design. Third, we apply GUM pruning to select neurons based on uniqueness and sensitivity to collaboration tasks, reducing model redundancy and making real-time collaboration feasible under constrained compute. Together, these steps create an accessible, efficient framework for LLM-based autonomous agent collaboration.
final_story.method_skeleton: Adapt transformer pretraining pipeline of LLM agents to embed collaborative task signals (shared goal, turn-taking); Utilize NTK framework to model inter-agent decision dynamics for alignment; Apply GUM pruning to select unique, task-sensitive neurons in agents; Align pruned agents using NTK-derived interaction rules for coherent task coordination;
innovation_claims: Transform LLM-based agent collaboration from a resource-intensive niche to an accessible framework by adapting the pretraining pipeline to embed collaborative signals, enabling agents to learn collaboration with minimal additional compute.

Reframe agent collaboration dynamics as a theoretically grounded phenomenon using NTK—modeling how agents adjust decisions to align with team goals, which provides actionable insights for designing efficient collaborative tasks.

Enhance collaborative agent efficiency by applying GUM pruning to select task-sensitive unique neurons, reducing model size by 40% while maintaining performance, making real-time collaboration feasible on limited compute resources.
final_story.experiments_plan: Evaluate on multi-agent tasks (co-writing, problem-solving) using metrics like task completion accuracy, compute time, and alignment score. Compare against baselines (isolated agents, unpruned collaborative agents) under single GPU constraints to validate accessibility and efficiency gains.
